extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of early-18th-century periodical essays (The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and interpreting early-18th-century Spectator essays by Addison that give moral and practical advice in short, didactic prose. Includes reflections on contentment, singularity, and the choice between temporal and eternal goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to acquire and judge contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Two practical means to acquire the virtue of Content: (1) always consider how much you have more than you want; and (2) consider how much more unhappy you might be than you really are. Content is equivalent to wealth; luxury is artificial poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and illustrative anecdotes are supplied: Aristippus's reply about farms ('I have three Farms still, and you have but one'), the honest Dutchman who after breaking his leg said 'It was a great Mercy that 'twas not his Neck', and an old philosopher whose guests would see their misfortune in perspective. The essay argues that contracting desires and reflecting on worse possible states alleviates murmur, repining, and inordinate ambition. Religious faith is recommended as the system that most effectually produces true, lasting contentment; other philosophical consolations may show that discontent is unreasonable but often fail to relieve it. Anti-patterns: fixating on losses, constantly comparing oneself to those richer, and chasing imaginary pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: When singularity (being different) is laudable versus vicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularity is laudable when, in contradiction to a multitude, it adheres to the dictates of conscience, morality, and honour; it is vicious when it makes people act contrary to reason or when it seeks distinction by trifles (dress, behaviour, small eccentricities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: the nature of actions, not the number of actors, should regulate behaviour; truth and duty trump custom. However, deference to custom is due in indifferent parts of life (dress, small manners), and excessive insistence on abstract reason in trivial matters renders one ridiculous or useless in society. Example: a gentleman who rigidly followed 'pure dictates of Reason' in trivial habits (mealtimes, phrases, dress, reciting Homer at the window) became socially ostracized and was legally treated as a lunatic despite doing no harm. Anti-patterns: affectation of oddity for its own sake; mistaking minor eccentricities for principled singularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer securing eternal/higher goods over temporal pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing between pursuing the pleasures and honours of this short, uncertain life and securing the pleasures of an eternal life, one ought to prioritize the other (eternal) life; it is folly to sacrifice the eternal for temporary gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses thought experiments (the sand-grain annihilation and comparison of durations) to show that even very long earthly spans pale beside eternity; reason may be misled by imagination into overvaluing near, long-seeming pleasures, but proper judgment shows virtue aimed at the permanent reward is the wiser choice. The essay notes that if virtue must make one miserable in this life (rare), enduring short-term discomfort for eternal happiness is still rational. Anti-patterns: arranging one's whole life as if this transient life were endless; neglecting spiritual preparation while pampering temporal desires.
